hints.junior: 250,000 rows joined into one string on the main thread froze the whole tab — no spinner, no scroll, nothing, for several seconds. Customers assumed the app had crashed.
hints.mid: The freeze isn't a correctness bug, the CSV comes out right — it's a where-does-this-run bug. Anything long and synchronous blocks layout, paint, and every event handler on the same thread.
hints.staff: Dev and QA datasets are almost always small, so this cost is invisible until a real customer's data is orders of magnitude bigger — the bug ships latent until someone's data grows into it.

hints.junior: The number in the corner ticks up on its own about ten times a second — click export in each mode and watch whether it keeps ticking.
hints.mid: This is a real CPU-bound export timed to run about a second, either directly on the main thread or inside an actual Web Worker created for this demo.
hints.staff: Try 'Cancel export' mid-run in the fixed mode — worker.terminate() actually stops it, which the broken mode's synchronous loop structurally cannot offer.

hints.junior: A Web Worker runs on a separate thread with no DOM access but full access to loops, strings, and Blob — let it build the CSV so the main thread stays free.
hints.mid: The worker can't trigger a download itself — it postMessages progress and a final result back, the main thread updates a progress bar and creates the actual download from that.
hints.staff: postMessage copies data via structured clone, it doesn't share it — for real scale, have the worker fetch its own data rather than copying an already-fetched array across, and use transferables for the return trip.

hints.junior: A worker has no DOM access, so it can't click a download link itself — that trigger always happens back on the main thread once the worker hands back the finished data.
hints.mid: Give export a real cancel button backed by worker.terminate(), and disable the trigger while one's in flight — a second click starting a second concurrent export is exactly what frustrated users do.
hints.staff: For millions of rows, avoid holding the full export as one in-memory string or Blob even inside the worker — stream it out in chunks via the File System Access API or a chunked ReadableStream instead.

sections.junior: Today's case is about a CSV export that froze an entire browser tab, because building a quarter million rows into one big string happened synchronously on the main thread, the same thread responsible for every click and repaint on the page.
sections.mid: A synchronous loop building a huge string blocks the one thread responsible for layout, paint, and every event handler — including the one that would show a loading state.
sections.staff: Dev and QA datasets are almost always small, so the synchronous cost stays invisible until a real customer's data is orders of magnitude larger and it ships with no load test ever catching it.

sections.junior: The fix is a Web Worker. It builds the CSV on a separate thread and sends progress updates back to the main thread, which stays completely free to keep the page responsive the whole time.
sections.mid: A worker can't trigger a download itself, so the main thread posts the export request, the worker posts progress back periodically, and the main thread builds the actual download from the final message.
sections.staff: postMessage copies data across the thread boundary by default — for genuinely large exports, prefer having the worker fetch its own data over copying an already-fetched array across.

sections.junior: Watch the heartbeat counter in the corner while you run the export in each mode, and see whether it keeps ticking or freezes.
sections.mid: This is a real CPU-bound export timed to run about a second, either on the main thread or inside an actual worker — the heartbeat count shows exactly how many ticks the main thread managed.
sections.staff: Try cancelling mid-run in the fixed mode — worker.terminate() actually stops it, something the broken mode's synchronous loop structurally can't offer.

sections.junior: Never build a large export as one synchronous pass on the main thread. Move it to a Web Worker, report progress back, and give people a real way to cancel it.
sections.mid: Move serialization into a Web Worker, report progress back, give the export a real cancel button, and for very large datasets stream the output instead of holding it all in memory.
sections.staff: Guard against a second concurrent export, and for very large datasets never hold the full result as one in-memory string — stream it out in chunks.
